blindSummary: This state/province sits on both sides of the country's protective-law gradient. It passed a state-level decree formally typifying transfeminicide in unit law, part of the wave of unit statutes (following another unit's March 2024 first-in-country definition) that recognise gender-motivated killing as an aggravated offence. Yet an international human-rights group's March 2025 country review lists this unit among the six units that have reformed nothing to create a legal gender-recognition procedure - a mismatch between symbolic criminal law and the administrative vacuum that leaves identity documents permanently unfixable and is the most visitor-relevant legal fact in the country. As with other units' transfeminicide statutes, national reporting finds the laws advancing 'in law but not in sentences', so they mark official climate rather than enforcement.

An international human-rights group's report (6 March 2024) on a neighbouring unit: no legal gender recognition procedure there exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment - the August 2023 killing of an activist remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from that unit's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Baseline for how a unit without any procedure behaves.

A national newspaper (24 July 2024): the capital city made transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years (a law approved 18 July 2024), in a setting documented as among the deadliest for trans people in the region; over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.
